Anesthesia for Cardiac Surgery on a Patient With Stiff Person Syndrome
Raquel Ferrandis, MD,* Javier Belda, MD, PhD,* Juan V. Llau, MD,* Carmen Belda, MD,*
and José A. Bahamonde, MD†
S
TIFF PERSON SYNDROME is a rare and incapacitating
illness, characterized by a pronounced involuntary stiffness
of the axial muscles and the extremities, which was described
in 1956 by Moersch and Woltman.
1 The principal electrophys-
iological and clinical signs are caused by continuous and si-
multaneous contraction of agonists and opposing muscles
caused by involuntary activation of the motor unit.
The etiology of the syndrome is not known. An autoimmune
origin is postulated, based on high titers of glutamate-decar-
boxylase antibodies, the association with autoimmune disor-
ders (particularly diabetes mellitus), the presence of other an-
tibodies, and a strong immunogenetic association. The
decarboxylase glutamate is the limiting enzyme for synthesis of
gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), and a reduction of GABA
levels in the brain has been observed in patients with this
syndrome.
2 In 1989, Lorish et al 3 established the criteria for
diagnosis of stiff person syndrome ( Table 1 ). No association
has been described with cardiac diseases. Treatment is based on
drugs that facilitate GABA neurotransmission, like diazepam,
baclophen, and vigabatrin (which increases GABA levels by
inhibition of GABA-transaminase). Immunomodulator agents,
plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulins appear to
offer a substantial improvement.
4
Since the ﬁrst description, very few cases have been de-
scribed in the literature. There are even fewer references to
anesthesia of patients with this syndrome
5-8 (6 cases in Med-
line, 3 of them of the same patient and 1 for a pediatric patient),
which makes it insufﬁcient to establish the existence of phar-
macologic interactions ( Table 2 ).
A case of anesthesia of a patient with stiff person syndrome
scheduled for double heart-valve replacement (mitral and aor-
tic) is presented. In this review of the literature, the authors
found no cases concerning the anesthesia or postoperative
management for cardiac surgery with or without extracorporeal
circulation.
CASE REPORT
A 44-year-old woman weighing 68 kg was scheduled to have double
heart-valve replacement surgery. Two years earlier, stiff person syn-
drome had been diagnosed in the patient, based on clinical, neurophys-
iologic, and analytic criteria. Clinically, she presented progressive
stiffness starting in the lower limbs, which impeded walking. The
electromyograph showed continuous muscular activity, despite her
attempts to relax. Motor unit potential was normal, without signs of
myopathy or neuropathy. In the immunologic study, the anti-glutamic
acid decarboxylase antibodies were positive at high values, both for
radioimmunoassay, 22,000 U/mL (normal values less than 100 U/mL),
and for immunohistochemical analysis, 32,000 U/mL (reference inter-
val below 2 U/mL). Before the operation, the patient was being treated
with 50 mg of diazepam every 8 hours and 4 mg of tizanidine (a
centrally acting alpha
2-adrenergic agonist for reduction of muscle tone
associated with spasticity) every 24 hours, enjoying a fully autonomous
life and only occasionally suffering muscular pain from spasms at the
extremities, mainly in the morning, before the ﬁrst dose of diazepam.
As well as the cardiopathy already referred to, she had atrial ﬁbrillation

that was being treated with oral anticoagulants (acenocoumarol),
digoxin, and amiodarone. The patient had no previous surgical or
anesthetic procedures.
The preoperative transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a rheumatic
mitral valvulopathy with severe stenosis (mitral area of 0.9 cm
2, max-
imum gradient of 19, medium of 9 mmHg), a middle mitral insufﬁ-
ciency (jet regurgitation area of 7 cm
2), and a middle aortic insufﬁ-
ciency, with preserved cardiac function (ejection fraction 70%). The
coronary arteries were normal. The respiratory function tests showed a
major pulmonary restriction (forced vital capacity of 1.52 L, with
forced expired volume in the ﬁrst second of 96%). A control electro-
myogram was performed, which fell within normal limits.
During the preanesthesia visit, the patient was advised that the oral
anticoagulants would be replaced by low–molecular-weight heparin on
the days before the operation. The remaining treatment was maintained
until the night before the operation, which was scheduled for the early
morning. She was directed to take 50 mg of diazepam in the morning,
2 hours before surgery.
On arriving in the operating room, the patient was asymptomatic,
although she had not taken the dose of diazepam prescribed for that
morning. Premedication of 10 mg of diazepam was given intrave-
nously, without clinically signiﬁcant effects on breathing rate and
consciousness. After monitoring, induction of anesthesia was per-
formed with 10 mg of midazolam, 0.6 mg of fentanyl, and 25 mg of
etomidate intravenously. Immediately after loss of consciousness, myo-
clonias were observed in all 4 limbs, predominantly at the distal end of
the extremities, which stopped spontaneously in about 30 seconds.
Pancuronium bromide, 8 mg, was administered for muscle relaxation.
Propofol and remifentanil were used in continuous infusion to maintain
anesthesia (the bispectral index was between 40 and 50). The response
to the “train of 4” in the ulnar nerve was 1 of 4 50 minutes after the
initial dose of pancuronium and was 4 of 4 at 115 minutes. A further
4-mg dose was administered 20 minutes before ending extracorporeal
circulation.
The operation proceeded without incidents. At the end of the sur-
gery, 5 mg of diazepam and 0.25 mg of fentanyl were administered;
remifentanil infusion was stopped 5 minutes later. The total time for the
surgery was about 200 minutes. The bypass time was 90 minutes with
75 minutes of aortic cross-clamp. The patient was transferred to the
critical care unit where sedation with propofol, orotracheal intubation,
and mechanical ventilation were maintained. With respect to manage-
ment of benzodiazepines, after an initial bolus of 10 mg of diazepam,
continuous infusion of 6 mg/h (144 mg/24 h) was started. Monitoring
of the “train of 4” was continued in the critical care unit ;a1o f4
response was observed 2 hours after the last dose of relaxant and 4 of
4 three hours later (5 hours after administration of the relaxant). No
reversal of neuromuscular blockade was used because no weakness was
observed when the weaning from mechanical ventilation was started.
From the hemodynamic perspective, the patient remained stable.

Propofol infusion was stopped 7 hours after admission to the critical
care unit, and the patient quickly recovered consciousness. She then felt
pain in her arms and legs, and mild contractions in a forearm and lower
limbs were observed but without spasms. For this reason, a bolus of 5
mg of diazepam and 3 mg of morphine was added to the continuous
infusion. Extubation was performed 8 hours after her admission to the
critical care unit, without incidents. Four hours later, she again suffered
moderate pain and mild stiffness in her legs, and 50 mg of oral
diazepam were given. Gradual reduction of intravenous infusion to a
level of 1 mg/h was started 30 minutes later and was stopped com-
pletely 24 hours after entering the unit. After the ﬁrst oral dose, the
preoperative dosage rate was restarted (50 mg every 8 hours). The
patient made no further reference to muscular discomfort or contrac-
tions. She was discharged from the unit on the third day after surgery
without further noteworthy incidents and resumed her normal course of
treatment.
DISCUSSION
There are very few references to anesthetic procedures on
patients with stiff person syndrome, and there are no reports of
heart surgery in the literature, with or without extracorporeal
circulation. This is no surprise because the syndrome is a rare
disease (in the last 25 years about 150 cases have been de-
scribed in the literature worldwide). Continuing studies are
being made of its etiopathology, and the clinical effect of
administering the majority of general anesthetics (both intra-
venous and inhaled) and muscle relaxants is unknown. In fact,
in the few reported cases of anesthesia in these patients, the
results observed are sometimes very disparate. In 5 cases,
6-8
postoperative recovery occurred without incidents, even with a
transitory improvement in spasms and muscle stiffness, which
were attributed to the residual effect of isoﬂurane and propofol
on the motor unit. On the other hand, in the sixth case de-
scribed,
5 postoperative weakness occurred despite appropriate
reversion of the muscle relaxant, and assisted ventilation was
needed for 48 hours.
In the present case, the diazepam dosage must be empha-
sized. First, the patient did not take the 50-mg oral dose
prescribed for the morning of the operation, for which reason a
dose of 10 mg was administered intravenously on her arrival in
the operating room, without incident. In the critical care unit,
because of an expected fast of more than 8 hours, oral admin-
istration was replaced with intravenous infusion, maintaining
the total daily dose of 150 mg. It seemed reasonable to maintain
the same diazepam dose to avoid withdrawal symptoms. As a
result, the patient showed no clinical symptoms, given that after
recovering consciousness the pain in the limbs suffered by the
patient was similar to that which she usually felt in the morn-
ings before taking her ﬁrst daily dose of diazepam. At no time
did the high diazepam doses cause secondary respiratory ef-
fects or depress her level of consciousness.
In addition, the pharmacodynamics of muscle relaxants on
these patients have not yet been described. In the published
cases
5-7 in which muscle relaxation was monitored, 4 opera -
tions (3 being on the same patient) in which vecuronium was
given and another on a pediatric patient, in which suxametho-
nium chloride was used, the effect of the relaxant used was
neither greater nor longer lasting. This was the expected result

because no effect on the neuromuscular junction has been
observed in stiff person syndrome. In the present case using 8
mg of pancuronium for intubation, the patient’s initial response
time to the “train of 4” and the time needed for its full recovery
were within normal ranges (coinciding with previous reported
cases). However, they were longer than the usual time ranges
after the second 4-mg dose administered before ending extra-
corporeal circulation. Nevertheless, new cases and more de-
tailed studies would be required to conﬁrm if there is a cause-
and-effect relation between extracorporeal circulation and the
longer effect of the muscle relaxant drugs.
With respect to the hypnotic drugs, those used in the cases
described in the literature (thiopental, propofol, isoﬂurane,
sevoﬂurane) showed no change in pharmacodynamics in these
patients. In the present case, however, myoclonias predomi-
nantly at the distal end of the 4 limbs were observed after
administering etomidate (a standard hypnotic for anesthesia
induction in cardiac surgery). It is already known that abnormal
movements, especially myoclonias, frequently appear after in-
jection of this drug in between 20% and 90% of cases accord-
ing to studies,
9 reﬂecting neuromuscular hyperexcitability,
which is the result of counteracting the inhibition caused by
subcortical activity. However, it has been observed that pre-
medication with fentanyl (10
/H9262g/kg intravenously) or diazepam
(150 /H9262g/kg intravenously) and atropine reduces the frequency
of these involuntary movements. 10 A reduction in these exci -
tatory phenomena has also been described with 10 mg of
diazepam when administered orally 1 hour before the anesthet-
ics.
11 In the present case, fentanyl and diazepam were both
given as premedication but did not prevent myoclonias. There
are insufﬁcient data to discern whether myoclonias are accen-
tuated by the basic illness and if they could have been avoided
with larger doses of benzodiazepines.
General anesthetics act by potentiating the GABA inhibitory
effect. Recent studies aimed at specifying the mechanism of
action of halogenated agents
12,13 found extended postsynaptic
inhibitory currents generated by GABA release (during a nor-
mal synaptic transmission). In these patients with reduced
GABA, the doses of anesthetic required (minimum alveolar
concentration, in the case of halogenated agents) or the time of
action could be expected to vary. There are no speciﬁc studies
on this point. Surprisingly, the standard doses administered in
the cases reported in the literature or in the present case did not
vary its effect.
To conclude, this is a pathology with numerous uncertainties,
especially with respect to management of anesthesia. Hence, ex-
haustive monitoring and follow-up of these patients are important,
adjusting the dosage of each drug to the individual response. With
Table 1. Criteria for Diagnosis of Stiff Person Syndrome
1. Prodromes centered on swelling and stiffness of the axial
musculature.
2. Slow progression to the point of affecting the musculature near
the extremities, making voluntary movements and walking
difﬁcult.
3. Deformity of the spinal column.
4. Intercurrent episodes of episodic spasms, precipitated by
brusque movements, sudden noises or emotional events.
5. Normal motor and sensory examination.
6. Normal intellect.

regard to preanesthetic management, the patient’s normal treat-
ment should be continued, emphasizing oral administration of the
ﬁrst morning dose and premedication with intravenous diazepam.
With respect to the hypnotic drug to be used, it is appropriate to
avoid those that lead to excitation and to maintain standard doses.
There appears to be no interaction with the muscle relaxants
(whether depolarizing or not) but individual monitoring of neuro-
muscular response is recommended (train of 4). During the post-
operative stay in the critical care unit, maintaining the preoperative
doses of benzodiazepines (by intravenous perfusion) suppressed
the patient’s symptoms without interfering with normal clinical
evolution or generating side effects.
